lessons.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
lessons.content: AI is the science of making machines that can think, learn, and decide. It's everywhere: voice assistants, recommendation systems, spam filters, self-driving cars. Narrow AI handles one task (chess, face recognition). General AI (human-level across all tasks) doesn't exist yet. AI works by processing large data and finding patterns humans might miss.
examples: Spotify recommends songs based on listening patterns
Google Translate handles 100+ languages
Self-driving cars detect pedestrians and signs

keyTerms.artificial intelligence: Machines that learn, reason, and decide from data
keyTerms.general AI: Hypothetical human-level AI across all tasks
keyTerms.intelligent agent: A system that perceives its environment and takes actions to achieve goals

lessons.title: History and Types of AI
lessons.content: AI began in the 1950s with Turing's 'Can machines think?' Early AI used human-written rules. Modern AI took off ~2012 with deep learning on GPUs. Types: rule-based (if-then logic), machine learning (learns from data), deep learning (multi-layer neural networks), reinforcement learning (trial and error). Key milestones: Deep Blue (chess, 1997), AlphaGo (Go, 2016), GPT/Gemma language models (2020s).
examples: 1997: Deep Blue beat chess champion
2012: AlexNet improved image recognition dramatically
2023: Language models write essays, code, answer questions

keyTerms.deep learning: Multi-layer neural networks learning complex patterns
keyTerms.neural network: Computing system inspired by the brain
keyTerms.machine learning: AI improving by learning from data
keyTerms.reinforcement learning: Learning through trial, error, rewards and penalties

lessons.title: AI Applications Today
lessons.content: AI transforms every industry. Healthcare: detecting cancer from scans. Agriculture: drones monitoring crop health. Education: adaptive tutoring (like AI Connect Africa!). Finance: fraud detection. Transportation: self-driving vehicles. NLP lets computers understand language — chatbots, translation. Computer vision lets AI 'see' — facial recognition, quality inspection. Generative AI creates text, images, code, and music.
examples: AI detects diabetic eye disease with 90%+ accuracy
Farmers identify crop diseases from phone photos
Banks flag suspicious transactions in real-time

lessons.title: How AI Models Work
lessons.content: AI models are mathematical functions that take inputs and produce outputs. They learn by adjusting internal parameters during training. Think of it like tuning radio dials until you get the clearest signal. Training process: feed the model thousands or millions of examples, it makes predictions, checks against the correct answers (loss/error), and adjusts parameters to reduce errors (gradient descent). After training, the model can make predictions on new, unseen data (inference). Models are only as good as their training data — biased or limited data produces biased or limited models. Larger models with more parameters can learn more complex patterns but need more data and computing power.
examples: Image classifier: trained on 1 million labeled photos → can identify cats, dogs, cars in new photos
Language model: trained on billions of text tokens → can generate coherent paragraphs and answer questions
Recommendation model: trained on user behavior → predicts what you'll want to watch next

keyTerms.training: The process of teaching a model by showing it examples and adjusting parameters
keyTerms.inference: Using a trained model to make predictions on new data
keyTerms.parameters: The internal values a model adjusts during training to improve accuracy
keyTerms.gradient descent: An optimization algorithm that minimizes prediction errors step by step

lessons.title: Large Language Models
lessons.content: Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT, Gemma, and Llama are AI systems trained on massive text datasets to understand and generate human language. They work by predicting the next word in a sequence — trained on billions of text samples from books, websites, and articles. LLMs can: answer questions, write essays and code, translate languages, summarize documents, and have conversations. They don't truly 'understand' — they recognize statistical patterns in language. Limitations: they can 'hallucinate' (generate plausible but false information), reflect biases in training data, and don't have real-time knowledge. Smaller models (1B-3B parameters) run on phones for offline use. Larger models (70B-400B) run on powerful servers. Fine-tuning adapts a general model for specific tasks.
examples: Gemma 3 1B: a small model running on your phone — powers AI Connect Africa's AI tutoring
GPT-4: a massive model (hundreds of billions of parameters) running on cloud servers
Fine-tuning: take a general language model and train it specifically on medical texts to create a medical AI assistant

keyTerms.hallucination: When an AI generates plausible-sounding but factually incorrect information
keyTerms.fine-tuning: Further training a general model on specific data for a specialized task

quiz.explanation: Fine-tuning adapts a pre-trained model: general model + medical data = medical AI.

quiz.explanation: LLMs are pattern matchers, not conscious understanders — they're very good at it but don't comprehend.

lessons.title: Collecting and Cleaning Data
lessons.content: Data is AI's fuel. Sources: surveys, sensors, websites, databases, social media. Raw data is messy: missing values, duplicates, typos, inconsistent formats. Cleaning fixes these: fill/remove missing values, remove duplicates, standardize formats. 80% of data science time is cleaning. Quality matters: garbage in, garbage out.
examples: Ages: 15, 16, '', 14, 999 — blank and 999 need cleaning
Mixed dates: '12/01/2024' and 'Jan 12, 2024' need standardizing
Duplicate entries with slightly different name spellings

keyTerms.data quality: How accurate, complete, and consistent the data is

lessons.title: Analyzing and Visualizing Data
lessons.content: Analysis finds patterns and insights. Descriptive stats: mean, median, mode, standard deviation. Visualizations make patterns visible: bar charts (categories), line graphs (trends), scatter plots (relationships), pie charts (proportions), histograms (distributions). Tools: Excel/Sheets for basics, Python (pandas, matplotlib) for advanced. Always ask: what story does this data tell?
examples: Line graph shows warming trend over 50 years
Scatter plot: more study hours → higher grades (positive correlation)
Bar chart: East region has highest sales

lessons.title: Databases and SQL
lessons.content: Databases organize large data efficiently. Relational databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite) use tables with rows and columns. SQL queries data: SELECT name FROM students WHERE grade = 'A'. NoSQL (MongoDB, Firebase) stores flexible documents. Cloud databases (AWS, Google Cloud) are accessible anywhere. Choose: structured data → SQL, flexible/rapid → NoSQL.
examples: SELECT * FROM products WHERE price < 100
School DB: tables for students, teachers, classes linked by IDs
Firebase: {name: 'Alice', age: 15, interests: ['math']}

lessons.title: Data Ethics and Privacy
lessons.content: Collecting data raises ethical concerns. Privacy: people should know what's collected and how it's used. Consent: users must agree before their data is used. GDPR (Europe), POPIA (South Africa) give people rights over their data. Data minimization: collect only what you need. Anonymization: remove identifying information. Data breaches expose personal information — companies must have security measures. Responsible data use means balancing innovation with protecting people's rights. Consider: just because you CAN collect data doesn't mean you SHOULD.
examples: GDPR requires websites to ask permission before tracking with cookies
Anonymization: replace names with IDs, remove addresses — data is useful but not identifiable
Data breach: a company's database is hacked, exposing millions of users' emails and passwords

lessons.title: Big Data and Data Pipelines
lessons.content: Big data refers to datasets too large or complex for traditional tools. Characterized by the 3 Vs: Volume (massive amounts — terabytes to petabytes), Velocity (data arriving at high speed — social media posts, sensor readings), and Variety (different formats — text, images, video, structured, unstructured). Data pipelines automate the flow: collect → clean → transform → store → analyze → visualize. ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) is the traditional process. Modern data lakes store raw data in any format for later analysis. Tools: Apache Spark for processing, Hadoop for distributed storage, cloud services (AWS, Google Cloud) for scalable infrastructure. Real-time processing handles streaming data (stock prices, social media feeds) as it arrives.
examples: Facebook generates 4 petabytes of data per day — traditional Excel can't handle this
A weather service: sensors → pipeline → clean → database → forecast model → app display
Real-time: stock trading algorithms process market data and execute trades in milliseconds

lessons.title: How Machines Learn
lessons.content: ML teaches computers to learn from data without explicit programming. Process: collect data → clean → split (training/test) → choose algorithm → train → evaluate → deploy. The model learns patterns. Overfitting: memorized training data but fails on new data. Underfitting: too simple to capture patterns. Cross-validation: test on different data splits for reliable evaluation.
examples: Show 10,000 cat/dog photos with labels → model learns to distinguish
Test on 1,000 unseen photos → measure accuracy
Overfitting: 99% training accuracy, 60% test accuracy

keyTerms.training data: Data used to teach the model
keyTerms.overfitting: Works on training but fails on new data
keyTerms.underfitting: Model too simple to learn the patterns
keyTerms.cross-validation: Testing on multiple data splits for robust evaluation

lessons.title: Supervised vs Unsupervised Learning
lessons.content: Supervised: labeled data with correct answers. Classification predicts categories (spam/not, cat/dog). Regression predicts numbers (price, temperature). Unsupervised: finds hidden patterns in unlabeled data. Clustering groups similar items (customer segments). Dimensionality reduction simplifies complex data. Semi-supervised uses small labeled + large unlabeled data.
examples: Supervised: emails labeled spam/not → predicts new emails
Regression: house features → predicts price
Clustering: customer purchases → discovers 3 segments

keyTerms.supervised learning: Learning from labeled data with correct answers
keyTerms.clustering: Grouping similar items together without predefined labels

lessons.title: Neural Networks
lessons.content: Neural networks: layers of connected nodes inspired by the brain. Input layer receives data, hidden layers find patterns, output layer gives predictions. Each connection has a weight adjusted during training. Deep learning uses many hidden layers. CNNs excel at images, Transformers at text/language. Training needs lots of data and GPUs.
examples: CNN: input image → edges → shapes → object identified
Transformer: processes entire sentences for context
Training GPT-like models needs thousands of GPUs for weeks

lessons.title: Model Evaluation and Metrics
lessons.content: How do you know if your model is good? Accuracy alone isn't enough — if 95% of emails are NOT spam, a model that always says 'not spam' has 95% accuracy but catches zero spam. Better metrics: precision (of predicted positives, how many are correct?), recall (of actual positives, how many did we find?), F1 score (balance of precision and recall). For regression: MAE (average error), MSE (average squared error), R² (how well model explains the data). Confusion matrix shows: true positives, false positives, true negatives, false negatives. ROC curve plots true positive rate vs false positive rate. Always evaluate on test data, not training data.
examples: Medical test: high recall is crucial — we'd rather flag healthy people (false positive) than miss cancer (false negative)
Spam filter: high precision is important — we don't want real emails marked as spam
Confusion matrix: 90 correct spam, 5 missed spam, 3 real emails in spam, 902 correct not-spam

keyTerms.precision: Of predicted positives, what fraction are actually positive
keyTerms.recall: Of actual positives, what fraction did the model correctly identify
keyTerms.confusion matrix: A table showing true positives, false positives, true negatives, false negatives

quiz.question: Why is accuracy alone misleading?
options: With imbalanced data, a useless model can have high accuracy
quiz.explanation: In imbalanced datasets (99% one class), predicting only that class gives 99% accuracy but is useless.

quiz.question: High recall is crucial when:
options: Missing a positive case is dangerous (cancer detection)
quiz.explanation: In medical screening, missing a disease (false negative) could be life-threatening.

quiz.question: Precision measures:
options: Of predicted positives, how many are actually positive
Of actual positives, how many were found
quiz.explanation: Precision = true positives / (true positives + false positives).

quiz.question: A false negative is:
options: A negative case the model missed
A positive case the model missed (predicted negative but actually positive)
quiz.explanation: The model said 'no' but the answer was 'yes' — a missed positive.

quiz.question: F1 score balances:
quiz.explanation: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall — useful when both matter.

lessons.title: Practical ML with Python
lessons.content: Python is the language of data science and ML. Key libraries: NumPy (numerical arrays and math), Pandas (data tables and manipulation), Matplotlib/Seaborn (visualization), Scikit-learn (machine learning algorithms), TensorFlow/PyTorch (deep learning). Typical workflow: import data (pd.read_csv), explore (df.describe(), df.head()), clean (drop nulls, convert types), visualize (plt.plot, sns.heatmap), split (train_test_split), train (model.fit), evaluate (model.score), tune (adjust hyperparameters). Jupyter Notebooks are ideal for iterative exploration — code, results, and notes in one document. Start with scikit-learn for classical ML; use TensorFlow/PyTorch for deep learning.
examples: import pandas as pd; df = pd.read_csv('students.csv'); print(df.describe()) — load and summarize data
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split; X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y)
model = DecisionTreeClassifier(); model.fit(X_train, y_train); print(model.score(X_test, y_test)) — train and evaluate

lessons.title: Bias in AI
lessons.content: AI reflects training data biases. Hiring AI trained on male-dominated data may prefer men. Facial recognition works worse on darker skin if trained mostly on light faces. Bias causes real harm: unfair loans, wrongful arrests, discrimination. Fight bias: diverse data, test across demographics, diverse teams, regular audits.
examples: Amazon scrapped biased hiring AI
Facial recognition higher error on darker-skinned women
Healthcare algorithm gave lower risk scores to Black patients

keyTerms.AI bias: Unfair results from biased training data or design

lessons.content: AI needs data but collecting personal data raises concerns. Privacy: people should know what's collected. Consent: users agree before data use. GDPR gives rights to access, correct, delete data. Deepfakes create fake realistic videos/audio. Responsible AI balances innovation with rights. Transparency: explain how AI makes decisions. Accountability: someone is responsible when AI causes harm.

Health app tracking location without telling users violates privacy

lessons.title: The Future of AI
lessons.content: Trends: AI in healthcare (drug discovery, early detection), climate (energy optimization), education (personalized learning), creativity (art, music, text). Jobs will change: some automated, new ones emerge. AI augments humans, not replaces. Most valuable skill: working WITH AI. Concerns: job displacement, autonomous weapons, power concentration. The future depends on choices we make today.

lessons.title: AI for Social Good
lessons.content: AI can address humanity's biggest challenges. Healthcare: AI diagnoses diseases in regions with few doctors — a phone app can detect skin cancer from a photo. Education: personalized learning for students who can't access good schools. Environment: monitoring deforestation from satellite images, predicting natural disasters, optimizing renewable energy grids. Agriculture: identifying crop diseases early, predicting weather for planting decisions. Accessibility: AI translates sign language, generates image descriptions for blind users, provides real-time captions for deaf users. Humanitarian: AI helps locate survivors after disasters, predicts refugee flows, and detects misinformation. The key is ensuring AI reaches the people who need it most, not just those who can pay for it.
examples: AI detects tuberculosis from chest X-rays in rural clinics without radiologists
AI-powered translation enables communication in 100+ languages including endangered ones
Satellite AI monitors illegal deforestation in the Amazon in real-time, alerting authorities

keyTerms.AI for good: Using AI to address social, environmental, and humanitarian challenges
keyTerms.digital divide: The gap between those with and without access to technology
keyTerms.inclusive AI: AI designed to benefit all people, not just privileged groups
keyTerms.humanitarian AI: AI applications in disaster response, refugee support, and crisis management

lessons.title: Building Your AI Career
lessons.content: AI careers are growing rapidly across every industry. Roles: data analyst (analyze and visualize data), data scientist (build predictive models), ML engineer (deploy and maintain AI systems), AI researcher (advance the field), AI product manager (guide AI product development), AI ethicist (ensure responsible AI). Skills needed: Python programming, statistics and math, data manipulation (Pandas, SQL), machine learning (scikit-learn), deep learning (TensorFlow/PyTorch), and communication (explaining results to non-technical people). Start with: learn Python, take an online course (Coursera, Kaggle Learn, fast.ai), build projects with real data, share your work on GitHub. You don't need a PhD — many successful AI practitioners are self-taught. The most important skill is curiosity: AI changes fast, so continuous learning is essential.
examples: Kaggle competitions: practice ML on real problems and compare with others worldwide
Portfolio project: build a model that predicts student exam scores from study habits — shows skills to employers
AI ethics role: review facial recognition deployment to ensure it works fairly across demographics

keyTerms.data scientist: Professional who extracts insights and builds predictive models from data
